Welcome, curious human

When did we stop playing?

I keep coming back to a question: when did we get so busy trying to optimise our lives that we forgot to play?

Aerial yoga was a bit of a lightbulb moment for me. I came for the movement, but what stayed with me was the chance to experiment, wobble, laugh and discover what my body could do. There was no particular outcome I was chasing.

But play isn’t always silly. It can be inventing a recipe instead of following one. Making your Tuesday lunch look beautiful just because you feel like it. Getting lost in a question, rearranging a room, or taking the long way home to see what’s there.

Of course, none of those things is automatically play. A beautifully plated dinner can be a delight or another standard to live up to. I’m interested in the difference: when does something feel free, absorbing, curious or simply fun to you?

That’s what we’re exploring here. Some ideas come from play research; others come from our own experiments. This isn’t another list of things to achieve. I hope you leave recognising more of the play that’s already yours.

Your Play History

Your play
story.

What if the things you loved as a child could tell you something about what brings you joy now?

Play researcher and psychiatrist Stuart Brown has spent decades exploring the role of play across our lives. One of the tools associated with his work is a play history: looking back at the games, adventures and interests that made us feel absorbed, curious and alive.

The idea isn’t to recreate your childhood. It’s to notice the threads: what drew you in, what you loved about it, what changed, and what might still be waiting for you.

We’ll guide you through four little chapters. At the end, you’ll have your own Play Story—a reflection of the patterns you notice, plus a keepsake you can save. No perfect memory required.

About 8–12 minutes · Skip any question · Save your answers privately as you go

Play Personality

What kind of
player are you?

Stuart Brown describes eight play personalities—different ways people are drawn to play, from storytelling and collecting to movement, creating and directing.

But I don’t think most of us fit neatly into one box. We’re combinations, and those combinations can change with context and time.

That’s why we created a playful, exploratory quiz inspired by his framework. You’ll discover your strongest play preferences, see how they overlap, and get a personalised collection of activities to try alone, with someone, or when you want to take it further.

Our quiz is in development and won’t be presented as a scientifically validated assessment.

The Fun Magnet Finder

Remember three to five times you had a genuinely wonderful time. Look beyond what you did: what made those moments feel so good to you?

The Fun Magnet Finder

Collect your good times.

Catherine Price describes True Fun as an experience of playfulness, connection and flow. But what creates those feelings is personal. Her approach invites you to recall several truly fun experiences and look for the people, activities, settings and qualities that keep showing up. We call those your fun magnets and fun factors.

Start with three memories. Add up to five. Look for patterns—not a diagnosis.

✳ The thinking behind this

Inspired by Catherine Price's The Power of Fun. The three components of True Fun provide the backdrop; this activity focuses on finding patterns across multiple enjoyable memories. The ingredient suggestions are ours, not a validated questionnaire. Explore her work ↗

A small shift in perspective

Could that be play?

Maybe you love tinkering with a recipe, styling an outfit, researching a strange little topic or arranging flowers. You might not call any of it play. But think about how it feels while you’re doing it.

Are you curious? Trying things out because you want to? Losing track of time? Enjoying the process even if the result is a bit wonky?

That’s worth noticing. And if it feels more like pressure than pleasure, that’s worth noticing too. The same activity can feel completely different on another day.

There’s no checklist that turns an activity into play. You get to investigate what it means for you.

THE PLAY ARCADETHIS
WAY ↗✳
Inspired by Ross Gay

The Wall of Joys.

In The Book of Delights, poet Ross Gay pays attention to small, often overlooked moments that delight him. Try noticing something unexpectedly lovely or funny in your day and saying “Delight!” when you catch it. Naming it can help you linger with it a moment longer. This wall is a place to keep those moments.

A little playful rebellion.

Catherine Price explores playful deviance in The Power of Fun: the pleasure of harmlessly bending expectations. Sometimes being told not to do something is precisely what makes it tempting. (We did warn you about the ducks.)

This is our explanation of Price's idea, not a direct quotation. Explore Catherine Price's work ↗
